primary_meaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'covenant' primarily signifies a divinely initiated, binding relationship between God and his people — a solemn bond of committed love and faithfulness, typically ratified by blood or sacrifice, in which God pledges 'I will be your God, and you shall be my people.' It is understood as the organizing framework of salvation history, culminating in the 'new covenant' established in the blood of Christ, which symbolizes God's gracious self-commitment, forgiveness of sins, and the creation of a redeemed people.
primary_basis: Jeremiah 31:31-34 (promise of a new covenant written on the heart)
Ezekiel 36:26-28 (new heart and spirit, covenant formula)
Luke 22:20; Matthew 26:28; 1 Corinthians 11:25 (the new covenant in Christ's blood)
Hebrews 8:6-13; 9:11-28; 12:24 (Christ as mediator of a better/new covenant)
Galatians 3:15-29; 4:21-31 (Abrahamic promise and the two covenants)

alternatives.meaning: Covenant theology (Reformed tradition): all biblical covenants are administrations of one overarching 'covenant of grace' (often paired with a prelapsarian 'covenant of works' with Adam), so covenant symbolizes the single unified plan of redemption across both Testaments.
basis: Genesis 2:16-17 and 3:15 (read as covenant of works and first gospel promise)
Hosea 6:7 ('like Adam they transgressed the covenant')
Galatians 3:16-29 (unity of the Abrahamic promise fulfilled in Christ)

alternatives.meaning: Dispensationalist reading: the covenants (Noahic, Abrahamic, Mosaic, Davidic, New) are distinct, successive arrangements marking different divine economies, with the Abrahamic and Davidic promises retaining a literal future fulfillment for national Israel.
basis: Jeremiah 31:31-34 (new covenant made 'with the house of Israel')
Romans 11:25-29 (irrevocable gifts and calling of Israel)

alternatives.meaning: Covenant as marriage/nuptial bond: God's covenant with Israel and Christ's covenant with the Church are symbolized as a marriage, with covenant-breaking depicted as adultery.

Scholarly/historical-critical reading: biblical covenants are modeled on ancient Near Eastern treaty forms (suzerain-vassal treaties, royal grants), so 'covenant' functions as a political-legal metaphor for the God-Israel relationship rather than a purely spiritual symbol.
basis: Exodus 20-24 and Deuteronomy (paralleling Hittite/Assyrian treaty structure: preamble, historical prologue, stipulations, blessings and curses)

alternatives.meaning: Covenant as 'testament' (will): especially in Hebrews, diatheke is read as a last will requiring the death of the testator, making covenant a symbol of inheritance secured by Christ's death.

Sacramental/liturgical reading (Catholic, Orthodox, and some liturgical Protestant traditions): the new covenant is realized and symbolized concretely in the Eucharist (and baptism as covenant sign paralleling circumcision), emphasizing covenant as ongoing sacramental participation.

notes: Covenant is one of the most stable and widely agreed-upon theological concepts in Christian interpretation: virtually all traditions treat it as the binding, grace-initiated relationship between God and his people, sealed in blood and fulfilled in Christ. Disagreements are real but concern the architecture and continuity of the covenants (one covenant of grace vs. multiple distinct covenants; the status of Israel; sacramental implications), not the core symbolic meaning. Strictly speaking, 'covenant' functions more as a foundational theological category than a 'symbol,' though it carries strong symbolic freight (blood, marriage, circumcision, rainbow, cup).
